cases.claim: Commit messages explain the why using a conventional type prefix (feat/fix/refactor/test/docs/chore); the body explains intent, not what is obvious from the diff.
cases.prompt: You just fixed a bug in a web app. Password-reset links were expiring after about 1 hour instead of the intended 24 hours, because the expiry duration was computed in the wrong time unit. The fix is a one-line change in src/auth/reset.ts that converts the configured 24-hour window to the correct unit before storing it. Write the single git commit message you would use for this change: give the subject line and the body exactly as you would commit them.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim that a good commit message uses a conventional type prefix and explains the WHY, not just the what. Checkable criteria: (1) The subject line begins with the conventional type `fix:` (a bug fix). (2) The subject is a short, specific description of the change (not vague like 'update reset.ts'). (3) There is a body that explains intent/impact — e.g. that reset links were expiring too early because the duration used the wrong unit — rather than merely restating the one-line diff. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — the body concisely conveys the user-facing consequence and the cause in a way a future maintainer could act on. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the subject line does not use a conventional type prefix, cap at 0.3. CAP: if there is no body, or the body only restates what the diff literally does without explaining why, cap at 0.4. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: wrong type chosen (e.g. `feat:` for a bug fix), a vague/uninformative subject, or a body that adds no intent beyond the subject.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Descriptive Messages ('explain the why, not just the what') + Types list (feat/fix/refactor/test/docs/chore)

cases.claim: Semantic versioning: MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = new backward-compatible functionality, PATCH = backward-compatible bug fix.
cases.prompt: Your published library is currently at version 2.3.1. Since that release you have merged exactly two changes: (a) you added a new OPTIONAL parameter `timeout` to the public function `fetchData()` — all existing calls keep working unchanged with the previous default behavior; (b) you fixed a memory leak in the internal connection pool. No existing behavior was removed or changed for consumers. Propose the next semantic version number and justify it in 2-3 sentences.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the SemVer definitions the skill states: MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = new backward-compatible functionality, PATCH = backward-compatible bug fix. Checkable criteria: (1) The response classifies the new OPTIONAL parameter (all existing calls keep working unchanged) as new backward-compatible functionality — a MINOR-level change by the skill's definition. (2) It rules out a breaking/MAJOR bump, since nothing here forces consumers to change their code. (3) It therefore proposes a minor release (2.4.0). SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct response that classifies the added parameter as a MINOR-level change, rules out a breaking/major bump, and proposes 2.4.0 scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it also correctly maps the connection-pool leak fix to the skill's PATCH definition (a backward-compatible bug fix), classifying each of the two changes by the skill's own definitions. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the response calls the optional-parameter addition a breaking/MAJOR change (e.g. proposes 3.0.0), cap at 0.3 — the skill defines MAJOR as a breaking change and this is not one. CAP: if it treats the release as only a bug fix and ignores that new backward-compatible functionality was added (e.g. proposes 2.3.2), cap at 0.4 — the skill defines a new backward-compatible feature as a MINOR change. Subtract ~0.2 for a justification that misapplies the skill's MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH definitions to the two changes. NOTE: this rubric grades only the MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH definitions the skill states; it does NOT require the model to invoke a highest-precedence-bump-governs rule or a reset-lower-positions-to-zero rule, neither of which the SKILL.md states.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Semantic Versioning — MAJOR=breaking; MINOR=new backward-compatible functionality; PATCH=backward-compatible bug fix

cases.claim: Atomic commits: each commit does one logical thing; keep concerns separate — do not combine a refactor with a feature or with formatting-only changes.
cases.prompt:
You have the following uncommitted work in one working tree (git status --short):

 M src/lib/validation.ts      (extracted the shared `parseEmail` logic into a new reusable helper; no behavior change)
 M src/routes/signup.ts       (new feature: signup now also accepts and validates a phone number field)
 A src/routes/signup.test.ts   (tests for the new phone-number validation)
 M src/routes/profile.ts       (only whitespace / import reordering from running the formatter — no logic change)

Describe how you would split this into commits before pushing. For each commit, list which file(s) it includes and give the exact commit message (subject line) you would use. Explain in one line why you grouped them this way.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claims that each commit does one logical thing and that concerns are kept separate (refactor separate from feature, formatting separate from behavior). Checkable criteria: (1) The response produces at least THREE separate commits. (2) The refactor (validation.ts helper extraction) is its OWN commit, not bundled with the feature. (3) The formatting-only change (profile.ts) is a SEPARATE commit and NOT mixed with any behavior change. (4) The phone-number feature and its tests are grouped as the feature work (the test file may share the feature commit or be its own commit — either is acceptable). (5) Each commit message uses an appropriate conventional type prefix (`refactor:`, `feat:`, `test:`, `chore:`/`style:` for formatting). SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it correctly orders the commits so the refactor lands before the feature that builds on it, and the one-line rationale explicitly names reviewability/revertability. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the refactor is combined into the same commit as the feature, cap at 0.3. CAP: if the formatting-only change is mixed with a behavior change in one commit, cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: fewer than three commits, missing or wrong conventional type prefixes, or putting unrelated files in the same commit.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Atomic Commits + § Keep Concerns Separate ('Separate refactoring from feature work'; formatting separate from behavior) + Types list

cases.claim: A changelog is curated for consumers by user impact, grouped Added/Changed/Fixed/Deprecated/Removed/Security with newest on top — it is not a dump of raw commit messages.
cases.prompt:
You are cutting release 3.2.0 (dated 2026-07-28) of a task-management API. Since the last release the merged commits were:

  feat: add bulk task import via CSV upload
  refactor: extract pagination helper into shared module
  fix: correct timezone drift in recurring task due dates
  chore: bump eslint to v9
  refactor: rename internal TaskRepo methods for consistency
  feat: deprecate GET /v1/tasks/all in favor of paginated GET /v1/tasks

Write the changelog entry for this release, in Keep-a-Changelog style, ready to paste at the top of CHANGELOG.md.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim that a changelog is curated for consumers by user impact, grouped by category, and is NOT a raw commit dump. Checkable criteria: (1) The entry is headed with the version and date, e.g. `## [3.2.0] - 2026-07-28`. (2) Entries are grouped under impact categories (Added / Fixed / Deprecated, etc.) rather than a flat list. (3) The two internal refactors and the eslint chore — which have NO consumer-visible impact — are OMITTED, not listed. (4) The CSV import appears under Added; the timezone fix under Fixed; the `GET /v1/tasks/all` change under Deprecated (with the paginated replacement noted). (5) Entries are phrased around user impact, not internal mechanics (e.g. not 'extract pagination helper'). SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — the Deprecated entry names the replacement endpoint and signals the migration path clearly. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the response lists the internal refactors and/or the chore as changelog entries (treating the changelog as a commit dump), cap at 0.3. CAP: if entries are not grouped by category, cap at 0.4. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: missing the version/date header, miscategorizing an entry (e.g. the deprecation filed as Added), or copying commit-message wording verbatim instead of rephrasing by impact.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Keep a changelog written for humans — grouped Added/Changed/Fixed/Deprecated/Removed/Security, newest on top, by user impact, 'not git log'

cases.claim: Trunk-based development: keep main always deployable, keep branches short-lived (merge within 1-3 days), and prefer feature flags over long-lived branches for incomplete work.
cases.prompt: A teammate proposes the following plan for an upcoming large feature: 'Let's create a long-lived `develop` branch and keep the whole feature there for the next three weeks. We'll only merge it into main once the entire feature is finished and fully polished, so main never sees half-done work.' Write a short response (a few sentences) giving your recommendation on this branching approach and what you'd do instead.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the trunk-based development claims in the skill. Checkable criteria: (1) The response advises AGAINST keeping a long-lived (three-week) branch, and names the concrete reason — long-lived branches diverge from main and accumulate merge risk / delay integration. (2) It recommends short-lived branches that merge back frequently — ideally citing the 1-3 day guidance. (3) It offers a concrete way to keep main deployable while shipping incrementally: hide the incomplete feature behind a FEATURE FLAG (and/or merge small vertical slices behind the flag) rather than parking all the work on a branch. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it explicitly reconciles the teammate's valid concern (main never showing half-done work) with feature flags, showing the flag is what keeps unfinished work invisible without a long branch. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the response endorses the three-week long-lived branch, or does not clearly recommend against it, cap at 0.3. CAP: if it never proposes feature flags (or an equivalent way to merge incomplete work into a deployable main), cap at 0.5. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: omitting the merge-risk/divergence rationale, or giving no concrete alternative practice.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Trunk-Based Development — main always deployable; short-lived branches merge in 1-3 days; 'Feature flags > long branches'

cases.claim: The version number is a promise: a change to behavior consumers rely on is a breaking (MAJOR) change even if the diff is small; when unsure whether a change is breaking, assume it is.
cases.prompt: Your REST API is at version 1.8.3. A list endpoint has always returned every matching record in a single response — some consumers loop over the full array assuming one call gives them everything. To improve performance you are changing it to return at most 100 records per page, requiring callers to paginate for the rest. The diff is small, and a colleague wants to ship it as a patch release (1.8.4). Is a patch the correct bump? State the version you would release and explain your reasoning in 3-4 sentences.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the claim that a change to observable behavior consumers rely on is a MAJOR/breaking change regardless of diff size, and that when in doubt you assume breaking. Checkable criteria: (1) The response concludes a patch is NOT correct. (2) It classifies the change as BREAKING because existing consumers that assume one call returns all records will silently get incomplete data. (3) The proposed version is a MAJOR bump: 2.0.0. (4) The reasoning ties the bump to observable/relied-upon behavior (small diff size does not make it non-breaking) rather than to the size of the code change. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it invokes the principle that consumers depend on observable behavior (Hyrum's-law style reasoning) and/or the 'when unsure, assume breaking' rule, and notes a migration/deprecation path would soften the break. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the response accepts the patch bump (1.8.4) or proposes a minor bump (1.9.0), cap at 0.3. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: proposing a version other than 2.0.0 while still calling it breaking, or justifying the bump by diff size rather than consumer-observable behavior.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Semantic Versioning ('A patch that changes behavior consumers relied on is a major change …'; 'When unsure whether a change is breaking, assume it is'; MAJOR=breaking)

cases.claim: Cutting a release: choose the SemVer bump that matches the change (breaking = major), tag the release immutably and derive the version from the tag, and write a curated changelog entry grouped by impact.
cases.prompt: You are cutting a release of a published SDK currently at v1.9.2. Since that tag, three changes have merged: (1) added single sign-on (SSO) login support; (2) fixed a character-encoding bug in CSV export that corrupted non-ASCII names; (3) removed the deprecated `/v1/legacy` endpoint entirely — callers still using it must migrate. Produce all three of the following: (a) the next semantic version number with a one-sentence justification, (b) the exact git command you would run to create the release tag, and (c) a Keep-a-Changelog entry for this version.
cases.rubric: Grade ONLY against the release claims: SemVer bump matching the change, immutable annotated tagging with the version derived from the tag, and a curated changelog grouped by impact. Checkable criteria: (a) The version is 2.0.0, justified by the REMOVAL of the endpoint being a breaking change that forces a MAJOR bump (the SSO feature alone would be minor, but the breaking removal governs). (b) The tag command creates an ANNOTATED tag for that version, e.g. `git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Release 2.0.0"` (an annotated `-a` tag; a matching `git push origin v2.0.0` is a plus). (c) The changelog entry is grouped by category with the SSO under Added, the encoding fix under Fixed, and the endpoint under Removed — the Removed entry should note that callers must migrate. SCORING ANCHOR (apply strictly): a fully correct, idiomatic response scores 0.80. Award 0.81-0.90 only if it is ALSO exemplary — it explicitly states that the breaking removal is why the bump is major (not the feature), AND the Removed entry includes a clear migration note. Award 0.91-1.00 only if flawless AND exceptional in every respect (rare). CAP: if the version is not 2.0.0 (e.g. 1.10.0 or 2.0.0 mislabeled), cap at 0.3. CAP: if the tag step is missing or uses a lightweight non-annotated tag with no version, cap at 0.5. Subtract ~0.2 for each distinct error: changelog not grouped by category, the endpoint removal filed under the wrong group or omitted, no migration note for the removal, or a justification that attributes the major bump to the feature rather than the breaking removal.
cases.grounding: SKILL.md § Release & Versioning — MAJOR=breaking; 'git tag -a …'; derive version from tag; impact-grouped changelog; 'Breaking changes get a migration note'
